newsitem.title: USA: Top enlisted man charged in U.S. Army sex scandal.
newsitem.headline: Top enlisted man charged in U.S. Army sex scandal.

text.p: The U.S. Army charged its top enlisted soldier with adultery and indecent assault against four military women on Wednesday in the latest chapter of a sexual harassment scandal that has rocked the service.

The Army said a senior officer would investigate the case against Gene McKinney, the only soldier who carries the venerated U.S. military title sergeant-major of the Army as leading member of the service's highest enlisted rank.
The investigator will decide if the 22-year veteran will face court martial.
He faces 18 sexual misconduct charges involving three Army women and a female sailor over a three-year period.

McKinney, 46, was suspended in February from his Pentagon job as the senior enlisted adviser to service leaders pending resolution of sex harassment allegations lodged against him by former Sgt. Maj. Brenda Hoster.

Hoster, who has retired after 22 years service of her own, alleges she resisted pressure from McKinney to have sex in a hotel room in Hawaii last year while his wife was in another room down the hall.

McKinney, also charged with maltreatment of soldiers and obstruction of justice, is assigned to administrative duties at nearby Fort Myer, Virginia. A base official said he would remain on the job pending a determination of whether any of the charges might be dismissed and whether he would be tried.
The McKinney case is the latest development in an Army sexual harassment scandal that includes charges of rape of women recruits by drill sergeants at several training bases.

Army Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson, a key figure in one of the worst U.S. military sex scandals, was sentenced on Tuesday to 25 years in prison for raping six women and other sexual offences at Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland.

The Army said the charges against McKinney included four counts each of indecent assault and maltreatment of soldiers, two counts of assault, one count of adultery, two of communicating a threat, two of obstruction of justice and three of soliciting adultery.
The incidents allegedly occurred between October 1994 and March of this year.
Details were not released, but Army investigators have questioned Hoster and the three other plaintiffs extensively.
Aside from the sexual harassment charges, conviction of adultery by itself is may be punished by jail and dismissal from the Army under the Uniform Code of Military Justice.
That code also prohibits sexual relations or even dating between troops of different rank.

Army Chief of Staff Gen. Dennis Reimer suspended McKinney from his Pentagon duties in February when the charges emerged, calling it "a dammed difficult decision, probably one of the most difficult decisions I've ever had to make."
Several Army trainers at Aberdeen and other posts have been convicted or entered guilty pleas in sexual harassment cases in the past several months.
Simpson was the first of 12 trainers charged with various acts of sexual misconduct at Aberdeen Proving Ground to go before a court-martial. He was charged with the most rapes.

His case is currently on automatic appeal. If that is rejected by higher courts, Simpson would be eligible for a clemency hearing in five years and for parole after serving eight years and four months.
